newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech banks say late subsidy not to affect profit.
newsitem.headline: Czech banks say late subsidy not to affect profit.

text.p: Czech banks Ceska Sporitelna a.s. and IPB a.s. said on Monday that the delayed payment of 800 million crowns in state subsidies on construction loans did not affect their 1996 earnings.
"The fallout of revenue will not show in the 1996 accounting," Sporitelna's spokesman Pavel Jirousek told Reuters.
Finance Minister Ivan Kocarnik said last week that postponing the transfer of the subsidies from the end of 1996 to this year was one of the measures taken to keep the 1996 state budget balanced.
Sporitelna, the country's largest savings bank, said that it had recieved its part of the payment, 397.5 million crowns, on January 5.
IPB's spokesman Jan Rezek confirmed his bank would do the same. "It will not cut into our (1996) result," he said.
The subsidy applies to cooperative and individual housing construction loans provided under communism and until the early part of the decade.
The state pays the banks the difference between the communist-era rates, of 1.0 to 2.5 percent, and the discount rate, which currently stands at 10.5 percent.

The governemnt took a number of measures, including spending cuts, freezing one billion crowns in infrastructure investment, and made early collection of 650 million owed by the Deposit Insurance Fund, to keep the 1996 budget balanced.
State accounting showed a 419 million crown surplus on December 31, but Kocarnik warned it might fall below zero as bills would keep coming until January 15.
